scenes.visual: Title card: One in Two Thousand.

scenes.tts: A mouse olfactory neuron carries about a thousand receptor genes, in each of its two genome copies. It uses one copy of one gene. How?
scenes.visual: A nucleus filled with about 2,000 small coloured tokens, in pairs. One token glows. On screen: about 1,000 genes, 2 copies each.
scenes.narration: A mouse olfactory neuron carries about a thousand receptor genes, in each of its two genome copies. It uses one copy of one gene. How?

scenes.tts: In nineteen ninety-four, Chess and colleagues, in Richard Axel's laboratory, made the puzzle sharp.
scenes.caption: In 1994, Chess and colleagues, in Richard Axel's laboratory, made the puzzle sharp.
scenes.visual: Title card: Chess and colleagues, 1994, Axel laboratory.
scenes.narration: In 1994, Chess and colleagues, in Richard Axel's laboratory, made the puzzle sharp.

scenes.tts: A neuron's receptor transcript comes from just one of its two alleles.
scenes.visual: Two copies of one receptor gene side by side, one maternal, one paternal. Only one emits RNA strands.
scenes.narration: A neuron's receptor transcript comes from just one of its two alleles.

scenes.tts: So the neuron faces about two thousand candidates. A mature neuron uses one, and keeps using it.
scenes.visual: The 2,000 tokens again; all dim except one, which stays lit as a clock runs.
scenes.narration: So the neuron faces about two thousand candidates. A mature neuron uses one, and keeps using it.

scenes.tts: This is called singular choice. One gene, from one allele, in nearly every mature mouse neuron.
scenes.visual: Label: singular choice = one gene, one allele, mature neuron (mouse).
scenes.narration: This is called singular choice. One gene, from one allele, in nearly every mature mouse neuron.

scenes.tts: It describes where development ends, not every stage on the way. Picture three broad phases.
scenes.visual: Three empty panels appear left to right: early progenitor, late precursor to immature neuron, mature neuron. Small label: broad phases, no sharp boundaries.
scenes.narration: It describes where development ends, not every stage on the way. Picture three broad phases.

scenes.tts: In early progenitors, the receptor genes are silenced, and little or no receptor RNA is detected.
scenes.visual: Panel 1 fills: every token grey, wrapped in dark chromatin. Label: early progenitor, silenced.
scenes.narration: In early progenitors, the receptor genes are silenced, and little or no receptor RNA is detected.

scenes.tts: From late precursors into immature neurons, several receptors are transcribed weakly. Single-cell data infer competing enhancer hubs.
scenes.visual: Panel 2 fills: three or four tokens glow faintly, then one grows brighter. Label: several, weakly, then one dominates.
scenes.narration: From late precursors into immature neurons, several receptors are transcribed weakly. Single-cell data infer competing enhancer hubs.

scenes.tts: In mature neurons, one gene from one allele is expressed, and feedback helps hold the choice.
scenes.visual: Panel 3 fills: one token glows brightly; a small padlock icon beside it. Label: one gene, one allele, kept.
scenes.narration: In mature neurons, one gene from one allele is expressed, and feedback helps hold the choice.

scenes.tts: Why is this hard? Suppose each gene had a small chance of escaping silence, independent of every other gene.
scenes.visual: Back to panel 1. Tokens flicker on at random, like popcorn.
scenes.narration: Why is this hard? Suppose each gene had a small chance of escaping silence, independent of every other gene.

scenes.tts: And suppose nothing afterwards shuts off extra genes or removes any neurons, and every neuron is counted at the same time. Then the number of escapes per neuron is close to a Poisson distribution.
scenes.visual: A bar chart: neurons with 0, 1, 2, 3 or more receptors. A slider labelled m, the average number of escapes. On screen: unregulated, unselected model, one observation time; P(exactly one) = m × e^(−m).
scenes.narration: And suppose nothing afterwards shuts off extra genes or removes any neurons, and every neuron is counted at the same time. Then the number of escapes per neuron is close to a Poisson distribution.

scenes.tts: You can set the average to anything. What is the largest fraction of neurons that can have exactly one receptor?
scenes.visual: The slider sits still. The exactly-one bar is highlighted with a question mark.
scenes.narration: You can set the average to anything. What is the largest fraction of neurons that can have exactly one receptor?

scenes.tts: In this model, about thirty-seven percent at most. The exactly-one bar peaks at an average of one escape per neuron.
scenes.visual: The slider sweeps from 0.1 to 3. The exactly-one bar rises to 37 percent at m = 1, then falls. On screen: maximum = 1/e ≈ 37%.
scenes.narration: In this model, about 37 percent at most. The exactly-one bar peaks at an average of one escape per neuron.
scenes.caption: In this model, about 37 percent at most. The exactly-one bar peaks at an average of one escape per neuron.

scenes.tts: Make escapes much rarer, and most neurons express nothing. Make them much more common, and most express two or more.
scenes.visual: Two frozen charts. m = 0.1: 90% none, 9% one. m = 3: 15% one, 80% two or more.
scenes.narration: Make escapes much rarer, and most neurons express nothing. Make them much more common, and most express two or more.

scenes.tts: Yet mature mouse neurons nearly all express exactly one. So this simple, unregulated model is insufficient.
scenes.visual: A real-neuron bar beside the model: almost all of it in the exactly-one column.
scenes.narration: Yet mature mouse neurons nearly all express exactly one. So this simple, unregulated model is insufficient.

scenes.tts: Mouse experiments support competition and receptor-dependent stabilization, but the arithmetic alone does not identify the mechanism.
scenes.visual: One token brightens; the tokens around it dim. Label: rules out the unregulated model only; mechanism not given by the arithmetic.
scenes.narration: Mouse experiments support competition and receptor-dependent stabilization, but the arithmetic alone does not identify the mechanism.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea for this lesson. Silence every gene, let a few compete, and lock in the winner.
scenes.visual: Callout card with the three phrases appearing one by one.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea for this lesson. Silence every gene, let a few compete, and lock in the winner.

scenes.tts: Repressive chromatin covers the receptor genes first. A few are transcribed weakly and compete at enhancer hubs.
scenes.visual: The three-phase panels again, with the first two highlighted.
scenes.narration: Repressive chromatin covers the receptor genes first. A few are transcribed weakly and compete at enhancer hubs.

scenes.tts: The leading gene's RNA helps quiet its rivals. Then its receptor protein sets off a stress signal.
scenes.visual: The brightest token sends out RNA and its rivals dim; then it emits protein and an alarm icon flashes.
scenes.narration: The leading gene's RNA helps quiet its rivals. Then its receptor protein sets off a stress signal.

scenes.tts: That signal turns down L S D one, an enzyme that new receptor expression depends on. Further escapes become rare.
scenes.visual: A key icon labelled Lsd1 fades. The grey tokens stay grey; the winner stays lit.
scenes.narration: That signal turns down Lsd1, an enzyme that new receptor expression depends on. Further escapes become rare.
scenes.caption: That signal turns down Lsd1, an enzyme that new receptor expression depends on. Further escapes become rare.

scenes.tts: Picture a library where every book is chained shut. A key frees a few, and they compete to be read.
scenes.visual: A library shelf of chained books. A key frees three of them.
scenes.narration: Picture a library where every book is chained shut. A key frees a few, and they compete to be read.

scenes.tts: The loudest reader drowns out the others. Then a bell rings and the key is taken away, so new books rarely open.
scenes.visual: One book is read loudly and the other two fall quiet; a bell rings and the key is lifted away.
scenes.narration: The loudest reader drowns out the others. Then a bell rings and the key is taken away, so new books rarely open.

scenes.tts: In the mouse, the chains are repressive chromatin. The key is a step that depends on L S D one. The bell is a stress pathway.
scenes.caption: In the mouse, the chains are repressive chromatin. The key is a step that depends on Lsd1. The bell is a stress pathway.
scenes.visual: Labels drop onto the library picture: chains = repressive chromatin; key = Lsd1-dependent step (candidate); drowning out = winner's RNA; competition = enhancer hubs; bell = stress pathway; bell plus key removed = the lock.
scenes.narration: In the mouse, the chains are repressive chromatin. The key is a step that depends on Lsd1. The bell is a stress pathway.

scenes.tts: The chapters ahead follow each step: the silence, the competing hubs, and the lock.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: unselected Poisson model, at most about 37% exactly one; experiments support mouse competition and feedback.
scenes.narration: The chapters ahead follow each step: the silence, the competing hubs, and the lock.

scenes.visual: End card: One in Two Thousand.
